videos.script: One chain of thought can take a wrong turn and still read perfectly. So ask for more than one. {{many}} Run the same prompt five times, with the temperature above zero. Each run draws different words, so each chain can take a different path. {{paths}} Read only the final answer of each. Three say fifty-four, one says sixty-six, one says forty-two. {{answers}} Take the answer that most chains reached. That is self-consistency: a vote among samples. {{vote}} The idea is that wrong paths scatter, and right ones meet at the same place. {{meet}} In this lesson you count a real vote, and then look at what it costs. Five samples is five times the bill. {{cost}} You will also see a vote that ties, and a vote where the majority is wrong. {{limits}}
